ABSTRACT
Tin-based perovskites are considered a promising alternative to lead-based perovskites due to their low toxicity and suitable optical bandgap.
However, the defects and voltage loss issues severely limit their device performance. In this study, an interfacial passivation strategy based on
pentylammonium acetate (PenAAc) was proposed in tin-based perovskite solar cells. The PenAAc-modified layer can effectively improve the
perovskite film morphology, crystallinity, and hydrophobicity. Meanwhile, the introduction of the PenAAc layer can significantly inhibit carrier
complexation and reduce the hysteresis effect in solar cells. By systematically analyzing the charge transport and compounding mechanisms,
the PenAAc layer enhances the built-in electric field, improves the carrier separation and the carrier extraction efficiency, and reduces the defect
density in the perovskite layer. The optimal tin-based perovskite solar cell achieved a power conversion efficiency of 7.0%. Moreover, the
PenAAc-modified device maintained above 89% of its initial efficiency even after 1200 h storage in a nitrogen-filled glovebox.

I. INTRODUCTION
Metal halide perovskite has been widely studied in the field of
photovoltaic materials due to its unique optical and electrical prop-
erties.1 Currently, the power conversion efficiency (PCE) of lead-
based single-junction perovskite solar cells (PSCs) has exceeded
26%, which is close to the Shockley–Queisser efficiency limit.2–4
However, the presence of elemental lead toxicity poses a threat to
the environment and human health, thus limiting its further com-
mercialization.5,6 Tin-based perovskites, particularly FASnI3, have
emerged as promising lead-free alternatives owing to their lower
toxicity, suitable bandgap, and theoretically high-efficiency poten-
tial.7 However, despite these advantages, tin-based PSCs still suffer
from severe voltage losses, poor morphology, and high defect den-
sities, resulting in PCE lagging far behind its lead counterpart.8–10
Developing effective passivation strategies is one of the effective
ways to enhance the photovoltaic performance of tin-based
perovskites.11–14 In recent years, interfacial passivation strategies have
been widely employed to improve perovskite film quality and device
performance. Chen et al. proposed a buried interface engineering
strategy utilizing an ultrathin 1-carboxymethyl-3-methylimidazolium
chloride (ImAcCl) modification layer for solving the problems of
Sn2+ oxidation susceptibility and defect density.15 Yan et al. utilized
a weakly polar solvent pretreatment strategy (WPSPS) to alleviate
the buried interfacial voids in tin-based perovskite and ultimately
resulted in high-quality tin-based perovskite films with low defect
density.16 Gao et al. introduced pentylammonium acetate (PenAAc)
molecules to modify the interface between the HTL and perovskite

excellent efficiency and improved stability were obtained.18 However,
there is still a lack of systematic exploration of defects and voltage

In this study, an interfacial passivation strategy based on
PenAAc was proposed in tin-based perovskite, which achieved a
suppressed defect density and reduced voltage loss. The effects of
the PenAAc passivation layer on film morphology, crystallinity,
and device performance were systematically investigated, and the
passivation mechanisms in devices were revealed by combining
space charge limiting current (SCLC), electrochemical impedance
spectroscopy (EIS), and deep energy level transient spectroscopy
(DLTS). Ultimately, the PenAAc-modified tin-based perovskite devices
achieved a PCE of 7.0% and maintained above 89% of its initial effi-
ciency even after 1200 h storage in a nitrogen-filled glovebox.

performed to explore the hydrophobicity of the perovskite films
[Figs. 4(c) and 4(d)]. The control device perovskite film showed a
contact angle of 65.88°, while the PenAAc-modified device perov-
skite film showed a contact angle of 72.80°. The results show that
the perovskite film of the PenAAc-modified device has improved
hydrophobicity in PSCs, which would increase the film stability
and the PSC stability. We further analyzed the film crystallinity
with an X-ray diffractometer (XRD) technique [Fig. 4(e)]. The dif-
fraction peaks at 14.4° and 28.6° in the XRD plots correspond to
the FASnI3 crystals with (100) and (200) lattice facets, respec-
tively.31 The diffraction peak intensities of PenAAc-modified
device films were significantly enhanced compared to the control
device films, which means that the PenAAc could improve the
crystallinity of tin-based perovskite films. This enhancement con-
tributes to the formation of denser perovskite films with fewer
pinholes.32 To investigate the defect states in the perovskite films,
we performed steady-state photoluminescence (PL) tests on perov-
skite films [Fig. 4(f)]. The photoluminescence intensity of the
PenAAc-modified film was higher compared to the control device,
which indicates that the defect states were suppressed.33
III. CONCLUSION
In conclusion, the deep-level defects and voltage loss in lead-
free PSCs were effectively reduced by introducing an interfacial pas-
sivation layer PenAAc. The PenAAc layer significantly suppressed
the density of defective states and facilitated efficient carrier separa-
tion and transport in the perovskite layer. The PenAAc-modified
device achieved a PCE of 7.0% and maintained above 89% of its
initial efficiency even after 1200 h storage in a nitrogen-filled glove-
box, exhibiting excellent interfacial stability. This work provided an
effective passivation scheme for the efficient lead-free PSCs.
